about.bio: Rojan Shrestha is a visual artist and photojournalist based in Kathmandu, Nepal, working across editorial, personal, and commissioned projects. Working primarily with the photographic image, his practice moves between documentary attention and more conceptual, staged work, across themes of memory, technology, identity, and space. Apart from his personal work, he has worked with Pahilo Post and Bizmandu, and contributes to NurPhoto, with work published by The Times UK, BBC, CNN, The Guardian, and The Wall Street Journal. As a photojournalist he covers politics, protest, social issues, and disaster in Nepal.

pieces.title: If you could do it all again
pieces.description: As technology advances, a new reality unfolds—a parallel universe known as the Metaverse, a virtual world that offers boundless opportunities yet poses a silent threat to human connection. In this space, people are drawn away from tangible interactions, spending more time in immersive digital environments that fulfill every social and personal need. The allure of the virtual world becomes so compelling that the physical world begins to feel distant, like a strange planet, leaving individuals confined to rooms that become their entire worlds. Through the lens of one individual's experience, this series explores the consequences of our growing dependence on immersive technologies that tempt us to forsake tangible reality for meticulously crafted digital environments. By blurring the boundaries between the physical and the virtual, these images explore how, despite advancements meant to connect us, technology may instead entrap us, severing the ties to our shared humanity. Are these shifts inevitable? And what happens when the allure of limitless digital freedom undermines our authentic connections?
pieces.metaDescription: Photographic series by Rojan Shrestha exploring the consequences of our growing dependence on immersive technologies.

pieces.title: Bitter Sugar
pieces.description:
In the midst of sweet sugarcane growing rigid and tall, the work ‘Bitter Sugar’ unveils the fragile lives of sugarcane farmers in the villages of Sarlahi district in the southern belt of Nepal.

Bitter sugar explores their relationship with their land, the burden of the debt, and the slowness of justice. Through the work, one sees that despite the callous disregard towards the hardships of the farmers and their families, they stand in resilience getting by each day working and being in togetherness.
